# Exact fixed-width cap optimization and the curvature budget

Fix positive concave widths `w_i`, on consecutive indices
`P={-L,...,R}` containing zero, with `sum_i i w_i=0`. Write
`M=sum_i w_i` and `Q=sum_i w_i^2`. We consider all convex-compatible
interval families of exactly these widths, with their true mixed centroid
at `(0,0)`, and the tested closed cap `H={x>=0}`.

## 1. Exact finite LP formulation

Write `K_i=[r_i-w_i,r_i]`. The family is convex-compatible if and only if

    Delta^2 w_i <= Delta^2 r_i <=0                     (1)

at every interior integer index. The true continuous centroid condition is

    sum_i w_i r_i=Q/2.                                 (2)

Necessity follows from convex lower and concave upper endpoints, and from
integrating x over each interval. Conversely, interpolate both endpoint
sequences linearly between integer indices. Conditions (1) make the lower
interpolation convex and the upper interpolation concave, so the region
between them is convex and has exactly the stated integer fibers. Its mixed
centroid is `(0,0)` by the two moment identities. With at least two positive
fibers this region is an ambient convex body. A single positive fiber can
be extended over a sufficiently short real base interval without introducing
another integer fiber.

Jensen gives

    r_0>=Q/(2M)>0,    r_0-w_0<=-Q/(2M)<0.              (3)

Thus the anchor is always properly cut. Concavity of r and convexity of
`r-w` imply that the proper indices form a consecutive block `[p,q]`
containing zero. Each nonempty tail outside that block is homogeneous:
wholly captured or wholly excluded. This also follows by intersecting the
convex hull with the line `x=0`, whose interior contains the centroid.

For every block `[p,q]` containing zero and every choice of captured/excluded
status for its two tails, form a linear program with constraints (1),(2) and

    r_i<=0                     on an excluded tail,
    0<=r_i<=w_i                on the partial block,
    r_i>=w_i                   on a captured tail.

Its objective is

    sum_(p<=i<=q) r_i + sum_(captured i) w_i.            (4)

The minimum over these finitely many LPs is exactly the least possible cap
mass among all the stated interval families. Closed inequalities in the
programs allow endpoint coincidences and cause only harmless duplication of
patterns. Every actual family belongs to a pattern, and every feasible
program vector gives an actual convex-compatible family and the objective
is exactly its cap mass. Each nonempty program has a finite nonnegative
optimal value attained by a feasible point: a linear functional with finite
infimum on a nonempty polyhedron attains it. Unbounded integer shears of r
therefore do not create a missing limiting family.

The program `../assets/pk-nov6/computations/fixed_width_true_centroid_cap_lp.py` implements this exact
formulation using floating-point linear optimization for falsification.
Its numerical outputs are not used as proofs of any universal inequality.

For a universal lower bound it is enough to consider symmetric partial
blocks `I={-h,...,h}`: the exact all-cusp angular reduction is proved in
`candidate bca993ec81e97cb4`. Caps with no captured
fiber are already handled separately by the quadratic width inequality.

## 2. An exact curvature identity on a symmetric proper block

Let `k=2h+1`, let T be the total width of the captured tails, and put

    c_j=-Delta^2 r_j,    d_j=-Delta^2 w_j,
    0<=c_j<=d_j.

For every interior index j define the two nonnegative call-function deficits

    kappa_j=sum_i w_i(i-j)_+ -M(-j)_+,
    tau_j=sum_(i in I)(i-j)_+ -k(-j)_+.                 (5)

Their nonnegativity is Jensen's inequality for the convex hinge and the
zero means of the width distribution and the uniform distribution on I.
Every sequence r has the exact representation

    r_i=r_0+b i-sum_j c_j[(i-j)_+-(-j)_+].              (6)

Indeed both sides have the same second differences and the same value at
zero; choosing b matches the remaining affine slope. Taking the w-weighted
sum and using (2) yields

    r_0=Q/(2M)+(1/M)sum_j c_j kappa_j.                  (7)

Taking the unweighted sum on the symmetric block eliminates b as well.
Consequently the ACTUAL cap mass obeys the identity

    F=T+kQ/(2M)+sum_j c_j[(k/M)kappa_j-tau_j].           (8)

No tail moments were discarded in this formula. In particular every such
cap has the proved lower bound

    F>=T+kQ/(2M)
          +sum_j d_j min{0,(k/M)kappa_j-tau_j}.          (9)

This bound may be weaker than the constrained optimum because setting each
c_j independently to an endpoint of `[0,d_j]` may violate the prescribed
cap-status inequalities. The formula does not assume those endpoint choices
are feasible.

## 3. Convex-order scope and the remaining term

If the width probability law `w_i/M` dominates the uniform law on I in
convex order, every coefficient in the final sum of (8) is nonnegative.
Then

    F>=T+kQ/(2M).                                     (10)

A sufficient condition is `w_i/M<=1/k` for all i in I. To see this, the
signed difference of the two laws is nonpositive on I and nonnegative
outside I, with total mass and mean zero. For every convex function phi,
subtract the affine secant line of phi through the endpoints of I. The
remaining function is nonpositive inside the interval and nonnegative
outside it; multiplying by the signed law and summing gives the claimed
convex-order inequality. For h=0 the uniform law is a point mass at zero,
and Jensen proves the same conclusion without a secant argument.

Equation (8) exposes the exact term missing beyond that regime: negative
call-function deficits can multiply available upper-boundary curvature.
One must control those terms together with cap-status feasibility and the
captured-tail budget. Simply discarding the term in arbitrary width families
is unjustified. This identity is not a general centroid-depth theorem.
